text.p: England's cricketers hit rock bottom in Zimbabwe, leaving captain Mike Atherton and coach David Lloyd facing their most critical tasks as they set off for New Zealand on Saturday.
A resounding defeat by 131 runs in the final one-day international on Friday was the ultimate humiliation for England, and gave Zimbabwe a 3-0 clean sweep in the series.

Atherton was facing the second leg of his team's assignment in defiant mood but the beleaguered skipper must be aware time for improvement is running out, with Australia arrving in England in May for a six-test Ashes series.

"I was appointed captain for the winter tour and that doesn't end here (in Zimbabwe), it continues to New Zealand," said Atherton. "Perhaps at the end I'll have to reassess but right now I'm looking forward to New Zealand."
Lloyd admitted England would be changing their strategy for limited overs cricket after losing the series to Zimbabwe.

"It's taught me that one-day cricket is very important. The tests were what we were here for really, but you can see the effect that playing well in one-dayers has on the confidence of the Zimbabwe guys," said Lloyd.
The two tests against Zimbabwe were rain-hit draws -- the second ending with the scores level -- and Atherton holds fast to his theory that England were robbed of victory by the weather.
He said: "We would have won in Bulawayo if the rain hadn't taken away a session and we were on top in the second test as well."

This hardly stands up to scrutiny. England were saving the game for three days in Bulawayo and were handed a chance to win because Guy Whittall became over ambitious and lost his wicket too soon after reaching a fine 50 on the last day.

In Harare, the touring side were bowled out for 156 in the first innings, and their inability to polish off Zimbabwe's tail on the final day left them with an awkward run chase in which they ended one short of victory.
The New Zealand itinerary includes three tests in which one of Atherton's priorities is to recover the form that has so often been a key element in England's performance.
His meagre record in Zimbabwe was 34 runs in four test innings and 66 in three one-dayers in which he dropped himself down the order.
Three players at least go to New Zealand with form and confidence intact.

Alec Stewart, effectively becoming the team's all-rounder again in his dual role as batsman-wicketkeeper, middle order batsman John Crawley and off-spinner Robert Croft, showing competitive instincts while establishing his credentials as a test bowler, achieved a measure of consistency.

England will welcome paceman Dominic Cork in New Zealand -- he missed the Zimbabwe leg to resolve personal problems -- but the crucial absence of a test-class bowling all-rounder still haunts the team.
Both Ronnie Irani and Craig White made ducks in the final match on Zimbabwe soil and neither did anything to make England look an even vaguely competent one-day side.
Perhaps the final word, reflecting the contrasting fortunes, should go to the souvenir seller at Harare Sports Club.
"I've sold out of Zimbabwe (replica) shirts -- all 7,000 of them. But I've still got 300 England ones left out of the 1,000 I had made up."
